title: Fisheries Off West Coast States; Modification of the West Coast Salmon Fisheries; Inseason Actions #6-#8
summary:
The government published two practical updates: one strengthens public access to information about hazardous chemicals stored at local facilities, and the other adjusts West Coast ocean salmon seasons midyear to keep catches within conservation limits.

For communities, the chemical update means you can ask your local emergency planning committee for a facility’s safety data sheets and annual inventory of hazardous chemicals. If they don’t have the records, they must request them from the facility and respond within set timelines. Fire departments can request on‑site inspections and must be told exactly where hazardous chemicals are stored. Companies can protect the actual name of a chemical if it’s a trade secret by sharing a descriptive category instead, and they can keep precise storage locations from the public, but they still have to provide those details to state and local officials and to fire departments. Residents and first responders benefit from clearer access to information that can help in planning and emergencies. Facility owners get clarity and some protection for proprietary information, but they face ongoing reporting duties, possible inspections, and tighter expectations about responding to information requests.

On the ocean salmon front, fisheries managers made three inseason moves. In California, several July and August recreational salmon dates were closed because anglers had already surpassed the summer target for Chinook. North of Cape Falcon, a short late‑June opening let commercial trollers harvest the little quota that remained from spring, capped at 10 Chinook per vessel. For July, managers set weekly per‑boat limits—first 60 Chinook, then 50—to spread out effort and keep the summer season within quota. These changes were announced quickly by hotline and Coast Guard radio because salmon move fast and conditions can shift within days. The aim is to protect fish populations and make the season last while staying true to conservation goals.

Who benefits? Communities and first responders gain better visibility into local chemical risks, and long‑term salmon health and future fishing opportunities are supported by careful catch limits. Who’s hurt or inconvenienced? Some facility operators may see more administrative work and inspections, and California anglers and coastal businesses lose planned fishing days. Commercial trollers face tight weekly limits that may not pencil out for every vessel.

What to do now: Facilities should double‑check their annual chemical reporting and be ready to respond to information requests. Community members can request safety data sheets and inventory details if they have concerns. Fishers should verify open dates and limits before heading out, since rules may change quickly to meet conservation targets.
